title: Canadian Silver Maple Leaf vs American Silver Eagle

segments.text: AMERICAN EAGLES COST MORE FOR IDENTICAL SILVER
segments.narration: American Silver Eagles cost more per ounce than Canadian Maple Leafs and the silver inside is nearly identical.

The Canadian Silver Maple Leaf contains .9999 fine silver, that is 99.99 percent pure. The American Silver Eagle is .999 fine, which is 99.9 percent. One extra nine. At current spot prices, the purity difference is worth less than a penny per coin. But the Maple Leaf holds the higher standard.
segments.explanation: The Canadian Maple Leaf is four-nines pure silver, slightly higher than the Eagle's three-nines standard.

segments.narration: The Silver Eagle is .999 fine, 99.9 percent pure. The coin weighs slightly more than a troy ounce because a copper alloy core adds durability. That extra weight is not silver. You are buying exactly 1 troy ounce of silver content per coin, same as the Maple Leaf.
segments.explanation: The American Silver Eagle is .999 fine silver, still investment-grade but one decimal below the Maple Leaf.

segments.narration: American Silver Eagles carry a premium of 4 to 8 dollars per ounce over the silver spot price for standard bullion. At 32 dollars spot, that puts the Eagle at roughly 36 to 40 dollars. The premium reflects USA Mint surcharges, an authorized dealer distribution layer, and strong domestic demand that keeps prices firm.
segments.explanation: American Silver Eagles typically cost $4 to $8 per ounce above the silver spot price.

segments.narration: Canadian Silver Maple Leafs run 3 to 6 dollars over spot for standard bullion. The Royal Canadian Mint uses a broader international distribution network with no USA-style surcharge structure. For buyers focused on getting the most silver per dollar, Maple Leafs typically win on entry cost.
segments.explanation: Canadian Silver Maple Leafs typically cost $3 to $6 per ounce above spot, $1 to $3 less than Eagles.

segments.narration: The gap between Eagles and Maple Leafs runs 1 to 3 dollars per ounce on average. On a 20-coin purchase, that is 20 to 60 dollars in real money. Over a year of monthly buying, it is hundreds of dollars in extra premium paid for identical silver content. That math matters for anyone building a position over time.
segments.explanation: The per-ounce price gap between Eagles and Maple Leafs adds up fast on larger purchases.

segments.narration: The Royal Canadian Mint launched the Silver Maple Leaf in 1988 at .9999 purity. Since 2014, every coin carries Bullion DNA authentication, radial line engraving and a micro-engraved maple leaf laser mark visible under magnification. The 2023 Mintshield surface treatment also addresses the milk-spot issue that plagued earlier coins.
segments.explanation: The Royal Canadian Mint has produced the Maple Leaf continuously since 1988, one of the oldest bullion programs.

segments.narration: The USA Mint has produced the Silver Eagle every year since 1986. In 2021, the Mint redesigned the reverse and added enhanced anti-counterfeiting features. American Silver Eagles remain the most-recognized silver coin in the United States and sell fast at local coin shops because American buyers specifically request them.
segments.explanation: The USA Mint has produced the Silver Eagle continuously since 1986, 40 years of unbroken production.

segments.title: TYPICAL PREMIUM OVER SPOT BY COIN TYPE
segments.narration: The chart shows typical dealer premiums per ounce by product type. American Silver Eagles carry the highest premium of any standard bullion coin. Maple Leafs track closer to generic rounds. Bars carry the lowest cost per ounce. Knowing these ranges before you buy means you can compare any two dealers in under a minute.
